1: Good morning. Thank you, Mister President and members of the jury. My name is Mouad Louhichi, and my thesis, supervised by Professor Mohamed Lazaar, is Cooperative Game Theory for Explainable AI in Recommendation Systems. It defends one idea: Shapley attribution is not only a post-hoc explanation. It can explain black-box clustering, stay consistent across levels, and finally guide what a recommender learns.
2: Seven parts. Each contribution follows the same order: gap, objectives, method, protocol, results, findings. Backup tables sit after the end, for questions.
3: Let me start with the introduction. Time check: minute 1.
4: Three questions frame the work. Everywhere: these systems shape what billions of people see, buy and watch. The black box: we see the output, not the reason. Trust: transparency should be built into the model, not added afterwards. So I treat accuracy and interpretability as two goals to meet together.
5: The whole thesis turns on this definition. An explanation is actionable when it names a factor you can change, when that change moves the output, and when the factor is stated in the domain's own terms. A chemical variable, a pollution indicator, a preference signal. Never a hidden latent code.
6: The context is the move from similarity models to hypergraphs. Matrix factorisation gave latent factors with no readable meaning. Graph models replaced the hidden code with a hidden message-passing mechanism. Hypergraphs added user-item-context relations but assume every message counts the same. Each step added power and removed transparency, while the EU AI Act and the GDPR ask for meaningful explanation.
7: Four familiar systems, and in each one the reasoning is hidden from the person it serves. Everywhere, and hidden: that is the gap this thesis targets.
8: Now the problem itself: the four approaches, their limits, the research questions. Time check: about minute 3.
ap_content: Four families, one slide each, because their limits motivate the thesis. Content-based filtering builds a profile from item features and recommends a match. It is explainable by construction: the reason is a named feature. Its limit is sameness, and it needs good metadata. That level of explanation, domain factors, is what I want to preserve.
ap_cf: Collaborative filtering ignores content and uses other users' behaviour. It is the base of matrix factorisation and of graph recommenders. Its weakness: new users and items have no history, and sparse matrices give little signal.
ap_hybrid: Hybrids mix the two signals and reduce cold-start. Matrix factorisation splits the interaction matrix into low-rank user and item factors. Accurate, scalable, still the standard baseline. But the factors are hidden: nobody can say what factor seven means. The field gained accuracy and lost the named explanation.
ap_graph: Graph and hypergraph models are the state of the art. Message passing moves information over several hops, and a hyperedge can join a user, an item and a context at once. The limit, in the orange box: they are costly, and they treat all messages as equally important. Contribution III challenges exactly that.
10: Four classical limitations: sparsity, cold-start, popularity bias, and the one this thesis targets, the lack of interpretability. For clustering it is harder still: methods give a local or a global explanation, not both, and they rarely stay consistent across levels of detail.
11: So three problems: models are hard to explain faithfully, local explanations do not scale to multi-level structure, and explanations never shape learning. The literature lacks one framework that does all three. My claim is that Shapley attribution can be that framework.
12: Five research questions. RQ1: can Shapley values explain black-box clustering faithfully? RQ2: does that extend to large-scale, multi-level clustering? RQ3: can attribution become part of how a recommender learns? RQ4: can it improve accuracy, context and diversity together? And RQ5, the thesis-level question: what do we gain by reading both tasks as one view?
13: Three contributions, one thread. C1 explains black-box clustering on wine quality. C2 scales the same logic to multi-level Beijing air-quality data. C3, the strongest claim, turns attribution into an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender. Cooperative game theory as one shared attribution view: explanation, then optimisation, then action.
15: Before the contributions, the shared experimental setup. Time check: about minute 7.
ds_wine: Portuguese white wines: four thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight samples, eleven laboratory measurements. Every column has a physical meaning, so when the explanation says density and pH, a wine maker knows what to do.
ds_beijing: Beijing air quality: three hundred and eighty-three thousand hourly records, six pollutants and five weather variables. Large, noisy, seasonal: the stress test for Contribution II.
ds_ml1m: MovieLens-1M: about one million ratings, six thousand users, three thousand seven hundred movies. The standard benchmark, so the numbers stay comparable with LightGCN, HCCF and HPCF.
ds_amazon: Amazon-Book: fifty-two thousand users, three million interactions, a density of six in ten thousand. It tests whether Shapley weighting helps most when the signal is weakest.
18: Splitting is designed against leakage. Clustering uses five-fold cross-validation. Recommendation uses a user-level, time-ordered split with a leave-one-out target and popularity-aware negatives. Five seeds, early stopping on validation NDCG.
19: For clustering, a LIME-based surrogate, the standard alternative to SHAP. For recommendation, six baselines from four families, with HPCF from 2025 as the strongest. I claim superiority only against the models tested here.
metrics: The metrics. NDCG at twenty is the headline. Coverage is the fraction of the catalogue ever recommended; intra-list diversity is the average dissimilarity inside one list, and it is built into the DyHuCoG utility, not only reported. For clustering, the Silhouette, which is also the value function of the clustering game.
20: Hardware, because it explains the runtime figures later: an Intel Core i9 for clustering, one RTX 4090 for DyHuCoG. Standard academic hardware.
21: Contribution I: explaining black-box clustering, answering RQ1. Time check: about minute 10.
22: Why start with clustering? The model creates its own structure, so the meaning of a cluster has to be worked out after the fact: the hardest test bed for attribution. The gap: methods give a local or a global explanation, rarely both, and local surrogates such as LIME carry no guarantee that the credit is fair or stable. There is no axiomatic way to explain a black-box partition in the original feature space.
23: RQ1 breaks into three objectives. A cluster-level explanation that keeps feature-level attribution; attribution in the original feature space, because that is what makes it actionable; and an argument for why Shapley is the right allocation rule rather than an ad-hoc surrogate.
dd_game: Three slides for the one mathematical object the thesis rests on. A cooperative game has players, coalitions, and a characteristic function v giving each coalition the value it creates alone. Take a three-piece band: alone they earn sixty, forty and twenty; Guitar and Voice together earn one hundred and forty, more than the sum; the whole band earns two hundred. Because of that synergy, a fair split must credit what a player adds to the others.
dd_shapley: Shapley's answer: let the players arrive one at a time in a random order, and pay each what they add on arrival. Averaging over the six orders gives ninety, seventy and forty, which sums exactly to two hundred. The four axioms, efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity, are why this is the right rule: Shapley proved it is the only rule satisfying all four.
25: So clustering as a cooperative game: the features are the players, and the value of a coalition is the Silhouette of K-Means run on that feature subset. But there are two to the power eleven coalitions, so we need a bridge. TreeSHAP explains trees, not centroids, and explaining the PCA space would move attribution away from the variables we care about. So K-Means gives labels, a LightGBM classifier learns to predict them from the original features, and TreeSHAP explains that surrogate exactly. The validity condition is surrogate fidelity: macro-F1 of about 0.82 is the floor.
c1_protocol: The protocol. K-Means plus-plus with k from two to ten, chosen by elbow, Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin and an interpretability check. A LightGBM surrogate with five-fold cross-validation, exact TreeSHAP in the original space, and a LIME surrogate on the same partition as the comparison. Success means the fidelity floor is met, the ranking is chemically meaningful, and the clusters have distinct signatures.
27: An honest point. I select three clusters on purpose, although the geometry prefers two: Silhouette 0.214 at k equals two against 0.144 at k equals three. I choose three because three clusters support three distinct, chemically meaningful wine stories, which is far more actionable.
28: The global ranking is led by density, then pH, fixed acidity, the sulfur dioxide variables and alcohol: exactly what a wine expert would name for structure, preservation and balance. The strip below is Figure 5.2, the per-cluster signatures. Each cluster has its own balance of the same small set of variables, so a cluster is not just a label, it is a distinct combination of drivers.
31: The answer to RQ1 is yes. Shapley values explain a black-box partition faithfully, provided the surrogate has high fidelity, and consistently at cluster level. On O3: SHAP satisfies the four axioms and gives local and global readings that compare across clusters; LIME fits a local surrogate with no such guarantee. One caveat: efficiency holds with respect to the surrogate output, not directly to the Silhouette game, which is why fidelity matters.
32: The partition is explained at cluster and instance level, in the original variables, with a chemically meaningful ranking and an axiomatic basis that LIME lacks.
33: The limits. The explanation depends on surrogate fidelity, not on the K-Means geometry directly. It is limited to tabular data. And it is single-level: it cannot yet say how importance changes between a partition and its sub-partitions. That last point starts Contribution II.
34: The takeaway: Shapley attribution is a well-founded lens for an unsupervised partition, and keeping it in the original feature space is what makes it actionable. But real data are rarely single-level.
35: Contribution II: scaling the explanation to multi-level, large-scale clustering. It answers RQ2, and the concern is not only scale but several levels of detail. Time check: about minute 20.
36: The gap. Once clustering is multi-level, feature importance must stay readable within a cluster, across sub-clusters and across levels. Three hundred and eighty-three thousand records cannot be explained coalition by coalition. A flat explanation may be true yet incomplete. And hierarchical clustering work gives no formal link between a parent's explanation and its children's.
37: RQ2 asks how the Shapley explanation extends to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying feasible and consistent. Three objectives. O1: a truly multi-level workflow with level-specific surrogates. O2: a formal cross-level consistency argument, Proposition 6.1. O3: validation at scale on data far from wine, the Beijing air-quality records.
38: The workflow is recursive: a coarse clustering on the full data, then each cluster split again. Each level gets its own surrogate and its own SHAP values in the same original space. The aggregation is not a naive average: a parent's attribution is a size-weighted expectation over its children. One point of method: the hierarchy is an analysis tool, not a claim that the data have a true natural hierarchy.
39: Contribution II: the same explanation at scale and across levels, answering RQ2. Time check: about minute 18.
c2_protocol: Same template on Beijing. Level one: K-Means plus-plus on the full data. Level two: each coarse cluster split again, three regimes into nine sub-clusters. One surrogate and exact TreeSHAP per level, aggregation by Proposition 6.1, and a sensitivity analysis over k, projection dimension and surrogate depth.
40: On Beijing the selection criteria agree strongly: three clusters, Silhouette about 0.63, Davies-Bouldin about 0.55, so the clusters rarely overlap. The two-component PCA view is for inspection only. The conclusions are robust to small changes in k, in projection dimension and in surrogate depth; only low-ranked variables shift.
41: RQ2 asks how the explanation extends to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying feasible and consistent. Three objectives: a truly multi-level workflow with level-specific surrogates; a formal cross-level consistency argument, Proposition 6.1; and validation on data far from wine.
43: The main payoff. At the coarse level, temperature and dew point dominate, because they separate the broad regimes. The force plots resolve three of them: a warm, sunlight-driven summer regime with ozone; a winter smog regime with carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulate matter under low wind; and a comparatively clean regime. Inside single clusters the informative variables shift. That is not a contradiction: the parent-level story is regime selection, the cluster-level story is variation within a regime, and Proposition 6.1 lets us read the shift as structure rather than noise.
45: The answer to RQ2 is yes, within bounds. Consistency is kept at scale and across levels, provided the hierarchy is modelled explicitly and the approximation is transparent. The bound is that this is still an explanation of a pre-computed partition.
46: The explanation scales because the hierarchy is explicit, Proposition 6.1 makes cross-level differences interpretable, and the logic transfers from four thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight wines to three hundred and eighty-three thousand air-quality records.
47: The limitations. The clustering stays static although the Beijing data are temporal. Surrogate-based SHAP with representative instances smooths out variation. And most important, the attribution is still post-hoc: it never influences learning. That is the bridge to Contribution III.
48: The takeaway: Shapley attribution stays consistent across levels of detail once the hierarchy is explicit, so explanations become interpretable at scale. But it still explains a partition that was already computed. Can cooperative attribution move beyond explanation and become part of how a recommender learns? That is Contribution III.
49: The third and main contribution: DyHuCoG, a Dynamic Hypergraph Cooperative Game, where Shapley attribution becomes an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender. It answers RQ3 and RQ4. Time check: about minute 27.
50: The gap. Graph and hypergraph recommenders treat message importance as uniform or attention-weighted, with no principled account of how much each user, item or context adds. Diversity is handled by re-ranking after training. Interpretability is added after prediction. And my first two contributions were still post-hoc. So the gap is a recommender that uses a cooperative-game utility, during training, to decide how much each player counts.
51: The gap. Every hypergraph recommender treats its messages as equally important, and attribution, when it exists at all, is computed after training. So the explanation describes a model it did not help build. The question is whether attribution can be part of the learning instead.
52: The game. Players are users, items and contexts, joined by hyperedges whose weights come from Shapley estimates. A coalition is the set of entities in one recommendation episode, and its value is the quality of what they achieve together. That value is explicit on screen: accuracy, diversity and context, weighted sixty, twenty-five and fifteen, plus a preference term. The trade-off the recommender must satisfy is the one attribution is computed from, so game and objective are aligned by design.
54: Exact Shapley is combinatorial, so we estimate it by Monte Carlo: over M sampled coalitions, average the value with the player minus the value without. The estimator is unbiased and its error falls as one over root M. We chose M equal to fifty, about ninety-nine percent accuracy, refreshed every ten batches and smoothed by an exponential moving average.
55: The architecture is the decisive move. Base propagation is standard hypergraph message passing; the Shapley-weighted version multiplies each message by a normalised Shapley coefficient. An attention gate blends that with the standard score as a stabiliser, and a context term is added. The last row is the training loss: BPR, plus diversity, plus context, plus regularisation. So the model optimises the same balance the attribution is computed from.
c3_protocol: The protocol. MovieLens-1M, dense, and Amazon-Book, sparse, with Yelp2018 as an extra check. Six baselines with HPCF as the strongest, four metrics, five seeds. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon on per-user NDCG with Holm-Bonferroni correction and Cohen's d. An ablation removes one component at a time. Success means beating HPCF on both datasets with corrected p below 0.05, coverage and diversity rising together, and overhead within about two times HPCF.
57: The headline result on MovieLens-1M, DyHuCoG in bold, best on all four metrics. HPCF reaches an NDCG of 0.2528; DyHuCoG gives 0.2775, plus 9.8 percent, and recall rises from 0.2098 to 0.2362. Coverage and diversity rise at the same time, because diversity is part of the coalition utility, not a re-ranking step. The gap widens from classical to graph to hypergraph, and DyHuCoG adds one more step. Standard deviations, in the backup, are about a tenth of the gap.
58: Same table, sparser data. Larger relative gains: plus 13.3 percent NDCG, plus 16 percent recall, coverage up nearly thirty percent. Absolute values are low for every model because the matrix is almost empty; what matters is the consistent ordering and the wider gap where data are weakest.
60: The ablation, per dataset. Context matters most: minus 8.2 and minus 11 percent. The hypergraph structure is second. Removing the Shapley weighting costs 4.6 and 6.1 percent, more on the sparser data. Every component contributes, and no single one explains the whole gain.
61: The cost, reported openly. DyHuCoG trains in about two thousand seconds against eleven hundred for HPCF, roughly 1.78 times. Inference is 1.84 milliseconds per query on MovieLens, well within real time. On convergence, M equal to fifty gives ninety-nine percent accuracy, so fifty is the right operating point.
62: Significance. Paired t-tests over six thousand and forty users, Holm-Bonferroni corrected. Against HPCF the t-statistic is 46.38 and Cohen's d is 1.33; Wilcoxon agrees. The effect size matters, because with six thousand users a tiny difference can look significant. Beyond accuracy, cold users gain about ten percent and cold items 9.6, and the gain holds on Yelp2018. These tests cover MovieLens-1M; Amazon-Book stays descriptive.
64: The answers. RQ3: yes, the Shapley estimates set the hyperedge weights while the model learns. RQ4: yes, ranking, coverage and diversity improve together on both datasets, with the largest gains where data are sparsest. All three objectives are met.
65: Attribution becomes part of how the recommender learns, the accuracy-diversity trade-off moves, and the improvement is statistically large.
66: The limitations, stated honestly. A compute overhead. A dependence on meaningful context, so on data without usable context the gain shrinks. A Monte Carlo estimator that could use variance reduction. An ablation that removes one component at a time. And baselines fixed in early 2026, so I claim superiority only against the tested models.
67: The takeaway is the conceptual shift of the thesis. Attribution is a first-class part of the learning objective, not a post-hoc check, so the explanation is a direct read-out of what the model optimises. That makes it faithful by design.
68: Let me bring it together. Time check: about minute 32.
69: Three contributions, one thread: explain, scale, guide. C1 explains a black-box partition in the chemistry. C2 keeps that explanation consistent across levels, with Proposition 6.1 as the formal argument. C3 carries the same logic inside the learning of a recommender. One definition, three value functions.
70: Three journal articles, all as first author: Procedia Computer Science in 2023, IJACSA in 2025, and IJIES in 2026 for DyHuCoG. IJACSA and IJIES are Scopus-indexed.
71: The limitations. On computation, exact Shapley is not feasible, so every contribution relies on approximation or surrogates. On method, the clustering chapters depend on surrogate fidelity and the recommendation results on meaningful context. On experiments, the clustering work is tabular and the recommendation work is offline, with no user study of actionability yet. And on the claim: not one unified framework that removes all tension, but a shared, well-founded view across both tasks.
72: Future work turns these limits into an agenda: lower-variance estimators and adaptive refresh rules; online and streaming recommendation with graphs that keep changing; user-centred evaluation of whether these explanations actually improve judgement and trust; and a broader trustworthy-AI evaluation including fairness.
73: To conclude. Cooperative game theory can serve as a shared methodological view for actionable explanation across clustering and recommendation. Four outcomes: Shapley attribution as a common formal language; three concrete achievements; explanation treated as method rather than as a comment added later; and a position aligned with the EU AI Act and the OECD principles.
